Ghṛta, the modern Ghee or ‘clarified butter,’ is repeatedly mentioned in the Rigveda and later both as in ordinary use and as a customary form of sacrifice. According to a citation in Sāyaṇa's commentary on the aitareya brāhmaṇa, the distinction between ghṛta and sarpis consisted in the latter being butter fully melted, while the former was butter melted and hardened (ghanī-bhūta), but this distinction cannot be pressed. Because the butter was thrown into the fire, agni is styled ‘butter-faced’ (ghṛta-pratīka), ‘butter-backed’ (ghṛta-pṛṣṭha), and ‘propitiated with butter’ (ghṛta-prasatta), and ‘found of butter’ (ghṛta-prī). Water was used to purify the butter: the waters were therefore called ‘butter-cleansing’ (ghṛta-pū). In the aitareya Brāhmaṇa^9 it is said that ājya, ghṛta, āyuta, and navanīta pertain to gods, men, Pitṛs, and embryos respectively.

Ghṛta-kauśika is mentioned in the first two Vaṃśas (lists of teachers) of the Mādhyaṃdina recension of the Bṛhadāraṇyaka upaniṣad as a pupil of pārāśaryāyaṇa.
